claims.text: Controlled SRO precipitates introduced into a PbTe-based compound will reduce its lattice thermal conductivity.
Heat in the initial PbTe-based thermoelectric material is carried primarily by lattice phonons.
The baseline material is a well-crystallized PbTe-based compound without intentionally engineered SRO precipitates.
Targeted thermal or chemical processing will be used to introduce SRO precipitates and control their size, spatial distribution, and interface quality.
Phonon transport is dominant in the proposed PbTe-based material at and above room temperature.
Engineered SRO precipitates act as nanoscale phonon-scattering centers.
SRO precipitates create discontinuities in the PbTe lattice structure.
The lattice discontinuities produced by SRO precipitates increase phonon-scattering events.
Increased phonon scattering reduces phonon scattering times.
Increased phonon scattering reduces the phonon mean free path.
Reduced phonon scattering times and mean free paths lead to lower lattice thermal conductivity.
The modified material will have measurably lower lattice thermal conductivity than the unmodified control.
The efficacy of conductivity reduction depends sensitively on precipitate size, concentration, spatial distribution, and interface coherency.
Precipitate characteristics outside optimal design parameters may limit or negate the conductivity reduction.
Analogous studies in similar systems support increased phonon scattering by SRO precipitates.
The quantitative conductivity reduction and the role of precipitate microstructure remain to be validated experimentally and computationally.
